title: Turn Research into a Written Brief and Audio Summary
summary: Turn checked research into a written brief and audio summary with versioned evidence, a spoken script, pronunciation review, and reliable delivery.
body_markdown:
Turning research into audio works best when the written brief is the source of truth. First establish what the evidence supports. Then adapt the approved brief for listening, generate the audio, and check that it preserves the facts and uncertainty. Sending raw search results straight to a voice model makes errors harder to find.


This reference workflow connects research, editorial review, and text-to-speech through a small set of tool capabilities. It can support founder briefings, internal market updates, or accessible versions of a research report. No paid audio was generated for this article, and the steps below are a design to implement and verify against the selected services.


## Define two deliverables with one evidence base


A written brief and an audio summary serve different reading conditions. The brief can contain links, tables, caveats, and detailed references. The audio needs a clear sequence, concise sentences, and spoken explanations of the information that matters. They should share a versioned evidence base rather than evolve independently.


Set the assignment explicitly. For example: produce a one-page update about a supplier’s product changes, plus a three-minute spoken summary for an internal team. Identify the decision the update supports and whether the listener needs a recommendation, a neutral recap, or an escalation.


Define what the audio may omit. It can skip a long URL or a table row that adds little to the spoken story. It should not drop a qualification that changes the conclusion. “The provider announced a feature” and “the feature is available in our account” are materially different statements in either format.


## Research into claims before writing prose


Gather primary sources and create a claim ledger. Each entry needs a fact, supporting URL, observation date, relevant passage, and status. Use unresolved and conflicting states so the writer can express uncertainty honestly.


[Exa’s contents reference](https://exa.ai/docs/reference/get-contents) documents retrieving material from known URLs. That is a useful capability after discovery has produced a bounded source list. Retrieve the pages needed for the assignment, then stop collecting once the important questions are answered or the research budget is reached.


Group the claims around the reader’s decision. A supplier update might distinguish changes to features, prices, access requirements, and migration work. This makes it easier to write a coherent brief and harder to bury a consequential limitation in an unrelated paragraph.


If a source cannot be accessed, preserve that gap. A confident voice can make uncertain material sound more established than it is.[The source-checking workflow](https://o11.ai/blog/source-checking-research-agent) provides a deeper method for checking the evidence before summarization.


## Approve the written brief before generating speech


Write the brief with a clear answer first, then supporting findings, implications, and open questions. Link factual claims near the relevant sentences. Label calculations, assumptions, and interpretations. Keep a stable revision identifier so the generated audio can point to the exact written version.


An editorial review should inspect high-impact claims, not just grammar. Verify names, dates, numerical comparisons, and claims that determine a recommendation. Check that the supporting source actually establishes each statement. Multiple articles repeating one announcement are not necessarily independent confirmation.


Use a small acceptance checklist: the central question is answered, material facts have evidence, uncertainty is visible, numbers reconcile, and there is no unsupported recommendation. If the brief fails, revise it before purchasing audio generation. This saves rework and prevents an attractive recording from becoming an excuse to retain a flawed script.


Store the approved text separately from drafts. A later edit to the research document should mark the audio stale rather than silently changing what its download link appears to represent.


## Write for the ear


Adapt the brief into a spoken script. Replace “see the table below” with a direct explanation. Introduce organizations before using acronyms. Turn compact written notation into unambiguous speech, particularly dates, currencies, and percentages. A listener cannot scan backward as easily as a reader can.


Keep the sequence simple: what changed, why it matters, what remains uncertain, and what the team should do next. Use transitions that identify the subject rather than relying on visual headings. Avoid a long list of URLs; tell listeners where the linked source document lives.


Create a pronunciation list for product names and technical terms.[ElevenLabs documents pronunciation dictionaries](https://elevenlabs.io/docs/api-reference/pronunciation-dictionaries/list) . Support varies by model and interface, so verify the selected operation before assuming it accepts a particular pronunciation control.


If a technical claim cannot survive simplification without changing meaning, keep a short accurate explanation in the recording and direct the listener to the detailed brief. Clarity is more useful than making every sentence sound effortless.


## Choose speech output for the delivery context


Pick the required file format, voice, language, and delivery method before generating. An internal downloadable briefing has different needs from interactive speech in a web application. Streaming can improve playback responsiveness, while a stored file makes versioning and review straightforward.


[OpenAI’s speech reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/audio/subresources/speech/methods/create) describes text input and audio output for its speech endpoint. A tool platform may expose a narrower input contract. Always inspect the operation available to the agent rather than copying provider-specific fields into a generic tool call.


Use an authorized voice and follow the selected provider’s requirements for synthetic-audio disclosure and voice rights. Choose a steady delivery appropriate to factual material. An overly dramatic reading can distort the apparent certainty or importance of a finding even if the words are unchanged.


For longer scripts, split at semantic boundaries and retain segment identifiers. This lets you repair one mispronounced paragraph without regenerating the entire brief. Join segments only after checking transitions, loudness, and pacing.


## Budget for revisions and listening


Estimate research, model inference, script revisions, speech generation, storage, and review separately. A speech price alone is not the cost of producing an accepted audio brief.


As an illustrative example, assume a 450-word script and a planning pace of 150 words per minute. The result is roughly three minutes, although actual duration depends on delivery. If two segments totaling 90 words need regeneration, the text sent for synthesis totals 540 words. Billing may use characters, tokens, duration, or another unit, so convert using the selected service’s documented model rather than treating words as its billing unit.


Cap revisions. Permit a pronunciation correction and a factual correction, then escalate unresolved issues rather than repeatedly generating slight variations. The goal is an accurate, usable briefing, not an indefinite search for a perfect voice performance.


The same cost model belongs in[multi-tool workflow estimation](https://o11.ai/blog/multi-tool-agent-cost-estimation) . Record discarded audio too, because it still consumed service usage.


## Verify the recording and handle partial failure


Listen to the entire recording before distribution. Pay special attention to proper nouns, decimals, dates, abbreviations, and sentences containing uncertainty. A successful audio response establishes that a file was produced, not that it says everything correctly.


Check duration, clipping, long silence, segment order, and whether the final words are present. Compare the audio against the approved script. Automated transcription can help identify differences, but an automatic transcript can repeat or normalize a spoken error. Human listening remains valuable for a short, important brief.


If speech generation fails, deliver the reviewed written brief and mark audio pending. If a job is still running, resume its existing status rather than creating another purchase. Preserve the job identifier and script revision. If the download expires, retrieve the existing result where supported before regenerating it.


Keep failure local. A voice problem should not invalidate correct research, and an inaccessible source should not be hidden because the speech file succeeded.[The asynchronous-job guide](https://o11.ai/blog/agent-async-image-video-jobs) covers durable media retrieval and recovery.


## Publish a traceable pair


Deliver the audio with a transcript, source brief, date, and revision. Label synthetic audio clearly where required and appropriate. For internal distribution, use the team’s authorized channel and access controls; creating a recording does not imply permission to email it to anyone.


When facts change, decide whether to replace the recording, append a correction, or retire it. Preserve enough history that a listener can understand which version informed an earlier decision. A concise correction is better than leaving a persuasive but outdated recording available without context.


Begin with one topic, a small source set, and one short recording. The useful automation is the reliable transformation from checked evidence to two accessible formats. Shared tool access reduces integration work, while the evidence and review process protect the quality of the result.


## Example: preserving a pricing caveat in audio


Suppose a fictional brief says a supplier introduced a new entry plan, while the available documentation leaves regional eligibility unresolved. The spoken summary should keep that limitation: “The supplier announced a lower entry price. We have not confirmed whether our account is eligible, so the team should verify that before changing its forecast.”


Removing the second sentence would make the recording smoother and the conclusion less accurate. The written source packet should identify the announcement, the eligibility gap, and the person responsible for checking it. The audio can direct listeners to that document for the detailed comparison.


Numbers deserve the same treatment. A written expression such as “1.5 million units” should not become “fifteen million” through an unreviewed script edit or pronunciation error. Keep a checklist of material figures and listen for each one in the final file.


This is also a useful correction exercise. Change one material fact in the written brief and verify that the package marks the dependent script and recording stale. A reliable workflow should make that dependency visible without regenerating unrelated sections or losing the previously approved evidence trail.
